list.snippet: Breast cancer is a disease where malignant (cancerous) cells develop in the breast tissue.
It typically occurs when cells in the breast start to grow and divide uncontrollably, forming a mass or tumor.
While most common in women, breast cancer can also rarely affect men.
The breast is made up of lobules (milk-producing glands), ducts (tubes that carry milk to the nipple), and connective tissue.
Breast cancer can begin in the ducts (ductal carcinoma) or lobules (lobular carcinoma).
The most common type is invasive ductal carcinoma, where cancer cells break out of the ducts and invade other breast tissue.
Cancer cells can spread through the lymphatic system, which is a network of vessels that help filter out bacteria and other foreign substances.
The closest lymph nodes to the breast are located in the armpit (axillary lymph nodes).
Breast cancer cells can enter these lymph vessels and potentially travel to other lymph nodes.
Cancer can also spread through the bloodstream to distant organs like the lungs, liver, brain, or bones.
Tumor Formation: Cancerous cells accumulate and form a mass or lump in the breast.

Changes in Breast Appearance: A lump, thickening, or swelling in the breast, changes in breast shape or size, skin dimpling, nipple inversion or discharge, or redness and swelling of the breast skin can be signs of breast cancer.
Metastasis: Spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body.
Certain factors can increase the risk of developing breast cancer, including family history, genetics, and lifestyle choices.
Having risk factors does not guarantee that a person will develop breast cancer, and people without risk factors can still be diagnosed with the disease.
Risk factors include:
Age: Risk increases with age.
Family History: Having close relatives with breast cancer increases risk.
Genetics: Certain gene mutations (like BRCA1 and BRCA2) can significantly increase risk.
Hormonal Factors: Early menstruation, late menopause, and hormone replacement therapy can increase risk.
Lifestyle Factors: Obesity, alcohol consumption, and smoking can also increase risk.
Ductal Carcinoma: Starts in the milk ducts.
Lobular Carcinoma: Starts in the lobules.
Inflammatory Breast Cancer: A rare and aggressive type where cancer cells block lymph vessels in the breast.
Other Types: Less common types include Paget's disease of the nipple and phyllodes tumors.
Treatment options vary based on the type and stage of breast cancer, and may include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, and targeted therapy.
Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer: This is the most common type, where hormones fuel cancer growth. Treatments can target these receptors, slowing or stopping cancer growth.
Early detection of breast cancer significantly improves treatment outcomes.
Regular breast self-exams, mammograms, and clinical breast exams can help identify breast cancer early.
